walkthroughs.body_html: Carbon is stored in four main reservoirs: the atmosphere (around 870 GtC as CO2), oceans (around 38,000 GtC dissolved), biosphere of plants and soils (around 2000 GtC), and lithosphere of fossil fuels and rocks (over 60 million GtC). Carbon moves between reservoirs as fluxes, in a balance that human activity has disrupted.

Major natural fluxes include photosynthesis (around 120 GtC/yr taken from atmosphere by plants), respiration and decomposition (returning a similar amount), and ocean-atmosphere exchange (around 90 GtC/yr each way). These fluxes were roughly balanced for millennia, keeping atmospheric CO2 near 280 ppm pre-industrial.

Burning fossil fuels and deforestation add around 10 GtC per year to the atmosphere. Oceans and land sinks absorb about half. The remaining 4 to 5 GtC accumulates each year, raising atmospheric CO2. Even modest-sounding fluxes accumulate quickly when natural sinks cannot keep up, driving climate change.
